messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 presentation to non-R users
messages.subject_clean: ggplot2 presentation to non-R users
messages.body_plain:
Thank you all for the good advice. It's definitely a challenge;
luckily the format is still open and as a first step I could in fact
simply provide some Sweave/beamer documents without doing an actual
presentation limited by inherent time constraints and diverging
interests. Once I have these written down, I'll have a better view on
what can spark the most interest.

Best,

baptiste

On Sun, Jul 31, 2011 at 12:56 PM, baptiste auguie
<bapt...@googlemail.com> wrote:
> Hi list,
>
> I've been asked to give a ~1 hour presentation at VUW on ggplot2 (+R)
> to physicists who know nothing about R and care little about advanced
> statistics. Most of them would typically use Origin/Excel to plot
> graphs; Excel / Matlab / Fortran / C for numerical simulations and
> data analysis. Any tips? Drawing from my own learning experience and
> interests, I'd like to discuss the following points by means of
> minimal visual examples, in a consistent story,
>
> - reproducible graphics. Use scripts as templates that can be re-used
> with new data.
>
> - grammar of graphics. Express graphics with a consistent and powerful
> language to map data and visual representation.
>
> - interactive data exploration. Using the grammar of graphics,
> coordinate transforms, aesthetic mappings and facets,
> multi-dimensional data sets can be better explored, more
> comprehensively, and rapidly.
>
> - good aesthetic defaults. How ggplot2 has been built with elegant and
> faithful graphic data representation in mind. (colour palettes,
> scales, automatic legend)
>
> - low level graphics control. Grid primitives, themes, custom grid
> plots and viewport integration.
>
> - Good choice of graphic devices. pdf, png, tikz. Animation, rgl.
> Multipage output. Sweave.
>
> - Data import and transformation. Custom import function for
> text-based data sets in multiple files. Parsing of strings, merging
> data sets. Transformation from wide/long format.
>
> - R for numerical calculations. Powerful combination of efficient
> mathematical routines (matrix operations, complex algebra, ...) and
> rich, expressive language (maximize code reuse, closures and lexical
> scope, apply family, ...)
>
> - Extensions to R. Highlight packages: plyr, reshape, Rcpp,
> RcppArmadillo, RcppEigen.
>
> - Making packages is easy. Interface with C/Fortran/C++ code.
> Namespace control. Documentation, examples integrated.
>
> - Open-source, vibrant community.
>
> I do realise this is too much stuff, especially since I like to
> present things as a unified story; any experience on what I should
> choose first? There's a tradeoff between getting people's attention on
> Yet Another Obscure Programming Language, and showing simple enough
> examples that they can actually reproduce, and get started quickly
> after the presentation.
>
>
> Best,
>
> baptiste
>

messages.subject: stacked bars, multiple layers + legend
messages.subject_clean: stacked bars, multiple layers + legend
messages.body_plain:
Trying to do a bar chart with

- change in GDP
- stacked contributions to GDP

I tried to do it with 3 layers
- GDP bars
- stacked positive contributions to GDP
- stacked negative contributions to GDP

It worked more or less OK until I tried to customize the legend, when I did that it went haywire. Got multiple legends, presumably for multiple layers. Also not sure if scale_colour_manual will let you specify color and fill independently for bars. Any way to make only the custom legend appear and fix the colors?

Not sure if I'm going about this all wrong, or if it's a bug or limitation, or missing something simple. Any pointers greatly appreciated.

library(quantmod)
library(ggplot2)
library(tis)

# get data statement
getSymbols("GDPC96", src="FRED")
getSymbols("PCECC96", src="FRED")
getSymbols("FPIC96", src="FRED")
getSymbols("CBIC96", src="FRED")
getSymbols("GCEC96", src="FRED")
getSymbols("NETEXC96", src="FRED")

# compute values
GDPC96_comp = GDPC96 - lag(GDPC96,1)
PCECC96_comp = PCECC96 - lag(PCECC96,1)
FPIC96_comp = FPIC96 - lag(FPIC96,1)
CBIC96_comp = CBIC96 - lag(CBIC96,1)
GCEC96_comp = GCEC96 - lag(GCEC96,1)
NETEXC96_comp = NETEXC96 - lag(NETEXC96,1)

# truncate
GDPC96_comp = GDPC96_comp['2008::']
PCECC96_comp = PCECC96_comp['2008::']
FPIC96_comp = FPIC96_comp['2008::']
CBIC96_comp = CBIC96_comp['2008::']
GCEC96_comp = GCEC96_comp['2008::']
NETEXC96_comp = NETEXC96_comp['2008::']

# make dataframe for pos values
PCECC96_pos<-PCECC96_comp['2008::']
PCECC96_pos[PCECC96_pos<0]<-0
FPIC96_pos<-FPIC96_comp['2008::']
FPIC96_pos[FPIC96_pos<0]<-0
CBIC96_pos<-CBIC96_comp['2008::']
CBIC96_pos[CBIC96_pos<0]<-0
GCEC96_pos<-GCEC96_comp['2008::']
GCEC96_pos[GCEC96_pos<0]<-0
NETEXC96_pos<-NETEXC96_comp['2008::']
NETEXC96_pos[NETEXC96_pos<0]<-0

PCECC96_posframe<-data.frame(PCECC96_pos)
PCECC96_posframe$date<-as.Date(rownames(PCECC96_posframe))
FPIC96_posframe<-data.frame(FPIC96_pos)
FPIC96_posframe$date<-as.Date(rownames(FPIC96_posframe))
CBIC96_posframe<-data.frame(CBIC96_pos)
CBIC96_posframe$date<-as.Date(rownames(CBIC96_posframe))
GCEC96_posframe<-data.frame(GCEC96_pos)
GCEC96_posframe$date<-as.Date(rownames(GCEC96_posframe))
NETEXC96_posframe<-data.frame(NETEXC96_pos)
NETEXC96_posframe$date<-as.Date(rownames(NETEXC96_posframe))

posframe <- PCECC96_posframe
posframe <- merge(posframe, FPIC96_posframe, by.x="date", by.y="date", all=TRUE)
posframe <- merge(posframe, CBIC96_posframe, by.x="date", by.y="date", all=TRUE)
posframe <- merge(posframe, GCEC96_posframe, by.x="date", by.y="date", all=TRUE)
posframe <- merge(posframe, NETEXC96_posframe, by.x="date", by.y="date", all=TRUE)
#fix dates to center quarters
posframe$date= posframe$date + 60

posmelt <- melt(posframe, id = 'date')

# make dataframe for neg values

PCECC96_neg<-PCECC96_comp['2008::']
PCECC96_neg[PCECC96_neg>0]<-0
FPIC96_neg<-FPIC96_comp['2008::']
FPIC96_neg[FPIC96_neg>0]<-0
CBIC96_neg<-CBIC96_comp['2008::']
CBIC96_neg[CBIC96_neg>0]<-0
GCEC96_neg<-GCEC96_comp['2008::']
GCEC96_neg[GCEC96_neg>0]<-0
NETEXC96_neg<-NETEXC96_comp['2008::']
NETEXC96_neg[NETEXC96_neg>0]<-0

PCECC96_negframe<-data.frame(PCECC96_neg)
PCECC96_negframe$date<-as.Date(rownames(PCECC96_negframe))
FPIC96_negframe<-data.frame(FPIC96_neg)
FPIC96_negframe$date<-as.Date(rownames(FPIC96_negframe))
CBIC96_negframe<-data.frame(CBIC96_neg)
CBIC96_negframe$date<-as.Date(rownames(CBIC96_negframe))
GCEC96_negframe<-data.frame(GCEC96_neg)
GCEC96_negframe$date<-as.Date(rownames(GCEC96_negframe))
NETEXC96_negframe<-data.frame(NETEXC96_neg)
NETEXC96_negframe$date<-as.Date(rownames(NETEXC96_negframe))

negframe <- PCECC96_negframe
negframe <- merge(negframe, FPIC96_negframe, by.x="date", by.y="date", all=TRUE)
negframe <- merge(negframe, CBIC96_negframe, by.x="date", by.y="date", all=TRUE)
negframe <- merge(negframe, GCEC96_negframe, by.x="date", by.y="date", all=TRUE)
negframe <- merge(negframe, NETEXC96_negframe, by.x="date", by.y="date", all=TRUE)
#fix dates to center quarters
negframe$date= negframe$date + 60

negmelt <- melt(negframe, id = 'date')

gdpframe<-data.frame(GDPC96_comp['2008::'])
gdpframe$date<-as.Date(rownames(gdpframe))+30
gdpmelt <- melt(gdpframe, id = 'date')

fullframe <- merge(negframe, posframe, by.x="date", by.y="date", all=TRUE)
fullmelt <- melt(fullframe, id = 'date')

# sort of OK without explicit legend params
ggp = ggplot(data=fullmelt, aes(x=date, y=value, color=variable, fill=variable, width=20)) +
    scale_x_date(expand = c(0, 0)) +
    xlab("
Source: US Bureau of Economic Analysis, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis") +
    ylab("$billions 2005 dollars") +
    theme_bw() +
    layer(data=gdpmelt,geom="bar", stat='identity', position='stack') +
    layer(data=posmelt,geom="bar", stat='identity', position='stack') +
    layer(data=negmelt,geom="bar", stat='identity', position='stack') +
    opts(legend.position="top", legend.direction="horizontal", plot.background = theme_rect(colour = 'black', fill = '#CCCCEE', size = 1, linetype='solid'))

#output
png(filename="/Temp/contrib.png", width=630, height=378, units="px")
ggp
dev.off()

# add legend, things get weird
ggp = ggplot(data=fullmelt, aes(x=date, y=value, color=variable, fill=variable, width=20)) +
    scale_x_date(expand = c(0, 0)) +
    xlab("
Source: US Bureau of Economic Analysis, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis") +
    ylab("$billions 2005 dollars") +
    theme_bw() +
    layer(data=gdpmelt,geom="bar", stat='identity', position='stack') +
    layer(data=posmelt,geom="bar", stat='identity', position='stack') +
    layer(data=negmelt,geom="bar", stat='identity', position='stack') +
    opts(legend.position="top", legend.direction="horizontal", plot.background = theme_rect(colour = 'black', fill = '#CCCCEE', size = 1, linetype='solid')) +
    scale_colour_manual(name="Contributions to GDP", breaks = c("GDPC96","PCECC96","FPIC96","CBIC96","GCEC96","NETEXC96"), values = c("black", "white","red","green","blue","yellow"),labels = c('GDP','Consumption', 'Fixed Investment','Inventories','Government','Net Exports'))

#output
png(filename="/Temp/contribng.png", width=630, height=378, units="px")
ggp
dev.off()

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the solution. I see one problem with the package you mentioned. It doesn't put the number between contour lines. please see the difference:

contour(volcano)

Moreover, it requires colour aes(colour = ..level..) though I don't want.
Using ggplot2 I wanted to get:

par(las=1, mar=c(2,2,0,0), mgp=c(2,.7,0), tck=-.01, cex=0.8)
contour(volcano, labcex = 0.8 )
abline(h=seq(0,1,0.2), v=seq(0,1,0.2), col="gray80")

Rob

2011/7/31 Ista Zahn <iz...@psych.rochester.edu>

> Hi Robert,
> While you can probably do this in ggplot2 with some effort, the
> directlabels package makes it really easy:
>
>
> library(directlabels)
> volcano3d <- melt(volcano)
> names(volcano3d) <- c("x", "y", "z")
> v <- ggplot(volcano3d, aes(x, y, z = z))
> v2 <- v + stat_contour(aes(colour = ..level..))
> direct.label(v2)
> direct.label(v2,"top.points")
>
> Note that this example is from
> http://rgm2.lab.nig.ac.jp/RGM2/func.php?rd_id=directlabels:direct.label
>
> Best,

Druce,

I'm not sure if I completely understand what you want in the end, but we'll give it a go.

fill and colour are two different scales and when you are trying to combine them manually into a legend you have to specify them both to be exactly the same to get them to unify. If that was what you were after then I think the following should work (might have to remove breaks put in by gmail).

Brandon

P.S. White bar + white background = invisible bars.

Source: US Bureau of Economic Analysis, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis") +

messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 presentation to non-R users
messages.subject_clean: ggplot2 presentation to non-R users
messages.body_plain:
On 7/30/2011 5:56 PM, baptiste auguie wrote:
> Hi list,
>
> I've been asked to give a ~1 hour presentation at VUW on ggplot2 (+R)
> to physicists who know nothing about R and care little about advanced
> statistics. Most of them would typically use Origin/Excel to plot
> graphs; Excel / Matlab / Fortran / C for numerical simulations and
> data analysis. Any tips? Drawing from my own learning experience and
> interests, I'd like to discuss the following points by means of
> minimal visual examples, in a consistent story,

One thing I didn't see in the list directly is LaTeX integration via
Sweave.  As physicists, they will already be conversant in LaTeX and
might appreciate tools that fit in that ecosystem better.

> - reproducible graphics. Use scripts as templates that can be re-used
> with new data.

And reproducible research in general.  I have long struggled with the
idea of what a "lab notebook" is in the context of computational
research/analysis.  Reproducible research is one answer to this
(probably coupled with version control and possibly some other things,
which get too far afield from your core point).

> - grammar of graphics. Express graphics with a consistent and powerful
> language to map data and visual representation.

This is a very powerful concept that is usable even outside of ggplot/R.
  Thinking about presenting data where an aspect (dimension) of the data
is represented by a visual aesthetic, and conversely being able to used
additional aesthetics to represent additional dimensions of the data, is
much different than most approaches.  I don't know which other programs
allow, say, shape or color to be determined by another variable.  Also,
physicists won't have a problem of thinking about this as a
multi-dimensional display; with two Cartesian dimensions, color and
size, you can display 4 continuous dimensions of data.  Faceting in two
directions and point shape give three more discrete dimensions.  Vector
fields give effectively two more dimensions.

> - interactive data exploration. Using the grammar of graphics,
> coordinate transforms, aesthetic mappings and facets,
> multi-dimensional data sets can be better explored, more
> comprehensively, and rapidly.

Interesting, but as Thomas pointed out, only if you actually do it
interactively, and I would add with a content relevant data set.

> - good aesthetic defaults. How ggplot2 has been built with elegant and
> faithful graphic data representation in mind. (colour palettes,
> scales, automatic legend)
>
> - low level graphics control. Grid primitives, themes, custom grid
> plots and viewport integration.

I wouldn't spend much time on this.  Yes, the defaults are pretty good.
  However what is even better is that any can be overridden.  The
details of how aren't all that relevant.

> - Good choice of graphic devices. pdf, png, tikz. Animation, rgl.
> Multipage output. Sweave.

<Tongue in cheek>
I don't care how many output formats it can do, so long as it does the
one I need.
</Tongue in cheek>

> - Data import and transformation. Custom import function for
> text-based data sets in multiple files. Parsing of strings, merging
> data sets. Transformation from wide/long format.

Data manipulation and management, especially in a reproducible way.  I
don't know how much of a core feature you would want to present versus
just something it can do in the course of other things.

> - R for numerical calculations. Powerful combination of efficient
> mathematical routines (matrix operations, complex algebra, ...) and
> rich, expressive language (maximize code reuse, closures and lexical
> scope, apply family, ...)

Matrix operations rest on LAPACK (not reinventing the wheel when it is
not needed).

> - Extensions to R. Highlight packages: plyr, reshape, Rcpp,
> RcppArmadillo, RcppEigen.
>
> - Making packages is easy. Interface with C/Fortran/C++ code.
> Namespace control. Documentation, examples integrated.
>
> - Open-source, vibrant community.

About these 3 together:  Open-source is something they probably already
care about or already decided they don't care about.  But the
interesting aspect is that expanding the abilities of R is not limited
to the commercial interests of any one company, but can be done by
anyone who has the need (and, of course, skill).  This is where the
interfacing to other languages (either package wrapping around, or
direct calls to and from) is interesting.

> I do realise this is too much stuff, especially since I like to
> present things as a unified story; any experience on what I should
> choose first? There's a tradeoff between getting people's attention on
> Yet Another Obscure Programming Language, and showing simple enough
> examples that they can actually reproduce, and get started quickly
> after the presentation.

This is really your core question: why are you giving the talk?  Are you
providing an introduction to a language/system that you would like
people to adopt?  Are you trying to give people tools that might be
useful in their work?  Are you showing people other tools just so they
know that they exist?  Are you trying to improve, either in terms of
ability or efficiency, existing practices?  Or another way of thinking
of the question, what do you want people to take away (know or do
differently) from your talk?

I think the two most generalizable topics are reproducible research and
the grammar of graphics.  These are not R/ggplot specific (though are
well supported by them) and so can be useful even using other tools.
Unfortunately, the two topics don't necessarily flow together well.

I gave a talk at our local R users group about ggplot; it is at
https://github.com/PortlandRUserGroup/Slides/blob/master/Diggs-ggplot2.pdf
  That may or may not be useful to you; the source Rnw file is there too.

Also, you mentioned making your presentation a Sweave/beamer document.
If you do so, one thing to point out is that the presentation is a
reproducible document itself.

> Best,
>
> baptiste

BTW, when I talk about physicists, I am speaking inclusively.  I am
(was?) a computational statistical physicist, but now I work as a
biostatistician.

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject_clean: Connecting points in paired measurements study
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I think this is the idea you're after. I put in colors for individual
IDs, but if you have a large number of them, it may well be better to
just stick with basic black. I'll show an example with and without
jittering to show you why you shouldn't jitter if you want to 'connect
the dots'.

df <- structure(list(id = c(17, 17, 122, 122, 125, 125), status =

structure(c(1L,
    2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L), .Label = c("BCR", "SRT failure"), class = "factor"),
        dt = c(56.5308871179212, 4.58145814023428, 8.58185033458939,
        100, 5.47125543964156, 14.0082396570109)), .Names = c("id",
    "status", "dt"), formats = c("%9.0g", "%11.0g", "%9.0g"), types = c(255L,
    251L, 255L), val.labels = c("", "Status", ""), var.labels = c("masterid",
    "", ""), version = 10L, label.table = structure(list(Status =
structure(c(1,
    2), .Names = c("BCR", "SRT failure"))), .Names = "Status"),
row.names = c("1",
    "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"), class = "data.frame")

# (1) Plot with jittering

ggplot(data, aes(x=status, y=dt)) +
    geom_point(size=4,colour="#000000",

                        position=position_jitter(width=0.05)) +
    geom_line(aes(group = id))

# (2) Plot without jittering, colored by ID
#       Use factor(id) for color to map individual colors to IDs
ggplot(df, aes(x = status, y = dt)) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = factor(id)), size=4) +
    geom_line(aes(group = id, colour = factor(id)))

In paired studies, it is often useful to plot one response against the
other, each (x, y) pair corresponding to a single respondent. One
qualitative measure of the efficiency of pairing is that the higher
the correlation between the response pairs across respondents, the
more 'efficient' is the paired design vis a vis an unpaired design. To
generate such a graph from the data, just recast it and then produce
the scatterplot:

dfm <- cast(df, id ~ status, value = 'dt')
ggplot(dfm, aes(x = BCR, y = `SRT failure`)) +
    geom_point(size = 4, color = 'black')

By using a colour aesthetic on the points, you can generate a legend
of IDs; alternatively, you could use geom_text() or the directlabels
package to label each point by ID. Clearly, the more pairs you have,
the less you would want to do this; OTOH, you may want to label
unusual points, in which case you could create a subset data frame for
them and then pass it into geom_text().

Hope you find something useful in this,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mauricio,

On Tue, Aug 2, 2011 at 12:01 PM, Mauricio <Maurici...@yahoo.com> wrote:
> I'm using "legend=TRUE" in geoms on chart, yet no legend is
> displayed.  Is that because 'y' is mapped in the geom functions
> instead of in the ggplot function?

No, it's because no aesthetic is mapped. To get the automatically
generated legend, you need to map a variable to an aesthetic.

>
> df <- data.frame(index=1:5, A=runif(5), B=runif(5))
> p <- ggplot(df, aes(x=index))
> p <- p + geom_point(aes(y=A), color="blue", legend=TRUE) +

> p <- p + geom_point(aes(y=B), color="green", legend=TRUE) +
> geom_line(aes(y=B), color="green", legend=TRUE)
> p

Try this:

dat <- melt(df, id = "index")
ggplot(dat, aes(x = index, y = value, color = variable)) +
geom_point() + geom_line()

Best,
Ista

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

You could also do this:

df <- data.frame(index=1:5, A=runif(5), B=runif(5))
p <- ggplot(df, aes(x=index))

p <- p + geom_point(aes(y=A, color="blue")) +
geom_line(aes(y=A, color="blue"))
p <- p + geom_point(aes(y=B, color="green")) +
geom_line(aes(y=B, color="green"))
p   # oops...

# Add the following to get the right colors
p + scale_color_manual('color', values= c('blue' = 'blue', 'green' = 'green'))

This indicates that mapping the colors one by one generates a factor
variable with the given colors as factor levels. As a result, you need
the manual scale to map the correct colors to the factor levels.

Ista's method is preferred and the way I would suggest to go. This is
an example where reshaping the data simplifies the ggplot() code
immensely, making it much easier to read and understand.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Is there trick to forcing legend when 'y' is mapped in geom (instead of ggplot)?
messages.subject_clean: Is there trick to forcing legend when 'y' is mapped in geom (instead of ggplot)?
messages.body_plain:
The usual way to merge two legends is to make sure they have the same
title, the same breaks and the same values (and if you change the
labels, they need to be the same, too).

Here's an 'easy' reproducible example: map the same factor to two aesthetics.

d <- data.frame(gp = factor(rep(LETTERS[1:4], each = 10)),
                 x = rep(1:10, 4),
                 y = rep(1:4, each = 10) +
                     rep(c(0.5, 0.7, 1, 1.2), each = 10) * rep(1:10, 4) +
                     rnorm(40))
ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y, colour = gp, linetype = gp)) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) + geom_line(size = 1) +
    labs(colour = 'Group', linetype = 'Group', y = 'Response')

Since the default title is the factor name 'gp', to change the title
to 'Group' in the merged legend I need to change the name of each
legend title. If you change one but not the other, you get two
legends; if the legends are given different names, you'll get two
legends.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
How's this for a solution?

x<-rnorm(1000)
h<-hist(x,30)

v<-vector(mode="numeric")
for (i in h$counts) {
 v<-c(v,i,i)
}
v<-c(0,v,0)
u<-vector(mode="numeric")
for (i in h$breaks) {
 u<-c(u,i,i)
}

d<-data.frame(u,v)

ggplot(d)+geom_polygon(aes(x=u,y=v),fill="white",color="black")+geom_hline(y=0)+theme_bw()

It's not very convenient, but I suppose it works.

- Dave

messages.subject: Re: Barplot with table but not with data.frame?
messages.subject_clean: Barplot with table but not with data.frame?
messages.body_plain:
Example:

> with(chickwts, table(feed))
feed
   casein horsebean   linseed  meatmeal   soybean sunflower
       12        10        12        11        14        12
> dd <- as.data.frame.table(with(chickwts, table(feed)))
> dd
       feed Freq
1    casein   12
2 horsebean   10
3   linseed   12
4  meatmeal   11
5   soybean   14
6 sunflower   12

In this simple one-factor case, table returns a named vector of
frequencies assigned a class 'table'. as.data.frame.table() takes the
table, converts the factors on each margin into variables (something
like expand.grid()), and creates a variable Freq to carry along the
cell frequencies. A more appropriate example in the multiway table
case would be UCBAdmissions, a 3D table. To convert it to a data
frame, use

as.data.frame(UCBAdmissions)

Dennis

I am curious to know how your presentation was. Can we get a copy of

On Jul 30, 8:56 pm, baptiste auguie <bapt4...@googlemail.com> wrote:

> Hi list,
>
> I've been asked to give a ~1 hour presentation at VUW on ggplot2 (+R)
> to physicists who know nothing about R and care little about advanced
> statistics. Most of them would typically use Origin/Excel to plot
> graphs; Excel / Matlab / Fortran / C for numerical simulations and
> data analysis. Any tips? Drawing from my own learning experience and
> interests, I'd like to discuss the following points by means of
> minimal visual examples, in a consistent story,
>
> - reproducible graphics. Use scripts as templates that can be re-used
> with new data.
>
> - grammar of graphics. Express graphics with a consistent and powerful
> language to map data and visual representation.
>
> - interactive data exploration. Using the grammar of graphics,
> coordinate transforms, aesthetic mappings and facets,
> multi-dimensional data sets can be better explored, more
> comprehensively, and rapidly.
>
> - good aesthetic defaults. How ggplot2 has been built with elegant and
> faithful graphic data representation in mind. (colour palettes,
> scales, automatic legend)
>
> - low level graphics control. Grid primitives, themes, custom grid
> plots and viewport integration.
>
> - Good choice of graphic devices. pdf, png, tikz. Animation, rgl.
> Multipage output. Sweave.
>
> - Data import and transformation. Custom import function for
> text-based data sets in multiple files. Parsing of strings, merging
> data sets. Transformation from wide/long format.
>
> - R for numerical calculations. Powerful combination of efficient
> mathematical routines (matrix operations, complex algebra, ...) and
> rich, expressive language (maximize code reuse, closures and lexical
> scope, apply family, ...)
>
> - Extensions to R. Highlight packages: plyr, reshape, Rcpp,
> RcppArmadillo, RcppEigen.
>
> - Making packages is easy. Interface with C/Fortran/C++ code.
> Namespace control. Documentation, examples integrated.
>
> - Open-source, vibrant community.
>
> I do realise this is too much stuff, especially since I like to
> present things as a unified story; any experience on what I should
> choose first? There's a tradeoff between getting people's attention on
> Yet Another Obscure Programming Language, and showing simple enough
> examples that they can actually reproduce, and get started quickly
> after the presentation.
>
> Best,
>
> baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Alpha and facet_wrap()
messages.subject_clean: Alpha and facet_wrap()
messages.body_plain:
I've struggled with geom_rect myself doing stuff like this (which is
intended to be a comment on me, not on geom_rect). The follow does
what you expect in the faceting case:

rect <- rbind(data.frame(xmin=0, xmax=8, ymin=0, ymax=100,foo = "a"),
              data.frame(xmin=0, xmax=8, ymin=0, ymax=100,foo = "b"))

ggplot(d) +
  geom_rect(data = rect,aes(xmin=xmin, xmax=xmax, ymin=ymin,
ymax=ymax),

            fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_point(aes(x=speed, y=dist)) +
  facet_wrap(~foo)

When doing things with geom_rect and faceting I nearly always resort
to building a separate data frame that explicitly contains the
faceting variable in it. I do this precisely because I haven't figured
out a way to avoid it, even when the rect is actually going to be the
same in each facet. My wild-ass guess is that this behavior has to do
with how ggplot makes guesses about how to draw the rect based on the
information you give it, specifically when you don't feed geom_rect a
distinct data frame so it's trying to fit that info into what it knows
about the data frame d.

Perhaps someone will chime in with a way to avoid this and we'll both
learn something...

messages.body_plain:
Hi Felipe,

Try this in a clean session with only one of gam or mgcv loaded mostly
because there is enough confusion of environments with ggplot2 calling
functions internally without adding that extra layer of masked
functions.  You also go to some unnecessary work to predict the
missing values.  I eliminate this.  Finally, I just use subset instead
of creating a special 'yes' 'no' column to indicate the missingness
that is already indicated by NAs in the 'passage' column.  Oh, and I
put the red points after the smooth so they show up better.

fishes <- structure(list(iddate = structure(c(1L, 12L, 14L, 15L, 16L,
17L, 18L, 19L, 20L, 2L, 3L, 4L, 5L, 6L, 7L, 8L, 9L, 10L, 11L, 13L), .Label
= c("1/1/2011", "1/10/2011", "1/11/2011", "1/12/2011", "1/13/2011",
"1/14/2011", "1/15/2011", "1/16/2011", "1/17/2011", "1/18/2011", "1/19/2011",
"1/2/2011", "1/20/2011", "1/3/2011", "1/4/2011", "1/5/2011",
"1/6/2011", "1/7/2011", "1/8/2011", "1/9/2011"), class = "factor"),
    passage = c(6L, 8L, 10L, 15L, 6L, NA, NA, 3L, 8L, 9L, 21L,
    8L, NA, NA, 34L, NA, 33L, 2L, 6L, 9L)), .Names = c("iddate",
"passage"), class = "data.frame", row.names = c(NA, -20L))

fishes$iddate <- as.Date(fishes$iddate, "%m/%d/%Y")

require(mgcv)
require(ggplot2)

m <- gam(passage ~ s(as.numeric(iddate)), data = fishes)
fishes$predicted <- predict(m, fishes)

ggplot(fishes, aes(x = iddate, y = passage)) +
  geom_point() +
  stat_smooth(method = gam, formula = y ~ s(x), size = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = iddate, y = predicted),
    data = subset(fishes, is.na <http://is.na>(passage)), colour = "red", size = 3)

HTH,

Josh

messages.subject: scales package and the development version
messages.subject_clean: scales package and the development version
messages.body_plain:
In the development version of ggplot2, are you expected to make your own
call to libarary("scales") to get certain things to work?  I was playing
with the new date scales and ran into problems with the examples when
scales wasn't loaded.

# To get the develop version on my system
# library("devtools")
# dev_mode()
library("ggplot2")
example("scale_x_date")

Gives the output:

 > library("ggplot2")
Loading required package: proto
 > example("scale_x_date")

scl_x_> # We'll start by creating some nonsense data with dates
scl_x_> df <- data.frame(
scl_x_+ date = seq(Sys.Date(), len=100, by="1 day")[sample(100, 50)],
scl_x_+ price = runif(50)
scl_x_+ )

scl_x_> df <- df[order(df$date), ]

scl_x_> dt <- qplot(date, price, data=df, geom="line") +
opts(aspect.ratio = 1/4)

scl_x_> # We can control the format of the labels, and the frequency of
scl_x_> # the major and minor tickmarks.  See ?format.Date and ?seq.Date
scl_x_> # for more details.
scl_x_> dt + scale_x_date()
Waiting to confirm page change...

scl_x_> dt + scale_x_date(labels = date_format("%m/%d"))
Error in structure(list(call = match.call(), aesthetics = aesthetics,  :
   could not find function "date_format"

date_format (and date_breaks used later in the example) are in the
scales package, but ggplot2 just imports scales, not depends on scales.

Are we expected to do our own loading of scales?  If so, should the
examples be changed to call scales:::date_format?

If I call

library("scales")

Then the example runs fine (*).

(*) [At least, it doesn't error due to that.  The example also contains
a melt, which is from reshape/reshape2 which is also just imported and
not attached.  When it gets to that, it errors.  Same problem, but
reshape/reshape2 is not coupled so tightly to ggplot2, that I would
expect that it must be available.  Still, the examples would need to be
changed so they run without error.]

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject: package:ggdendro to plot dendrograms and tree plots using ggplot
messages.subject_clean: package:ggdendro to plot dendrograms and tree plots using ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Dear ggplot community

I am very pleased to announce that I have published my package
ggdendro on CRAN and github.

The package description:  "This is a set of tools for dendrograms and
tree plots using ggplot. The ggplot philosophy is to clearly separate
data from the presentation. Unfortunately the plot method for
dendrograms plots directly to a plot device without exposing the data.
The ggdendro package resolves this by making available functions that
extract the dendrogram plot data."

CRAN: http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggdendro/index.html
github: https://github.com/andrie/ggdendro

An example:

	library(ggplot2)
	library(ggdendro)
	hc <- hclust(dist(USArrests), "ave")
	hcdata <- dendro_data(hc, type="rectangle")
	ggplot() +
	    geom_segment(data=segment(hcdata), aes(x=x0, y=y0, xend=x1,
yend=y1)) +
	    geom_text(data=label(hcdata), aes(x=x, y=y, label=text, hjust=0),
size=3) +
	    coord_flip() + scale_y_reverse(expand=c(0.2, 0))

Regards

Andrie

messages.subject: Faceted plot with horizontal bars; can it be done?
messages.subject_clean: Faceted plot with horizontal bars; can it be done?
messages.body_plain:
Hi people,

# I'm trying to produce a faceted plot with horizontal bars and I
# can't seem to get what I want. If you copy and paste everything below you'll
# get one plot containing my three attempts. For more detail see comments below.

# Here's my working example:

require(ggplot2)

# fake data
dat <- data.frame(
  type = c(rep("Veg", 4), rep("Fruit",2)),
  item = c("Potato", "Spinach", "Red onion", "Mixed leaves", "Tomato", "Lime"),
  proportion = c(0.03, 0.35, 0.95, 0.2, 0.57, 0.01)
)
dat$item <- reorder(dat$item, dat$proportion)

# First off, it's easy enough to produce the dot plot of what I want, so let's
# do that:

p.dot <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = proportion, y = item)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(type ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free") +
  opts(title = "Good, but I want bars not dots")

p.dot

# However, what I'm really after is a bar version of 'p.dot', so instead of dots
# we have horizontal bars starting out from zero. I can try and get this by
# doing something similar and using coord_flip():

p.bar <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = item, y = proportion)) +   # x and y are opposite
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip() +
  facet_grid(type ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free") +
  opts(title = "Ugh, what's with all the inappropriate levels?")

p.bar

# As you can see it's almost there, but for some reason it's put all the levels
# in for each category, we didn't have that problem in 'p.dot'

# By removing the coord_flip() and swapping bits around in facet_grid() I can
# get a vertical version of what I want:

p.bar.vert <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = item, y = proportion)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_grid(. ~ type, scales = "free_x", space = "free") +
  opts(title = "Good, but I want it rotated 90 degrees")

p.bar.vert

# This is perfect, except I want it rotated 90 degrees, how should I go about
# it?

# For those who copy and pasted everything or if you want to see all three at
# once
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(1,3)))
pushViewport(viewport(layout.
pos.col = 1))
print(p.dot, newpage = FALSE)
popViewport()
pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.col = 2))
print(p.bar, newpage = FALSE)
popViewport()
pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.col = 3))
print(p.bar.vert, newpage = FALSE)
popViewport()

# P.S. With 'p.dot' there also seems to be something wrong; there's white space
#      between the tick marks of 'Tomato' and Lime' and the plotting area

# What I'm using:
# Ubuntu 10.04, R version 2.13.1, ggplot2 version 0.8.9

If you really already have pre-summarized data, here is another work around:

GeomHbar <- proto(Geom, {

   default_stat <- function(.) StatIdentity
   default_pos <- function(.) PositionIdentity
   default_aes <- function(.) aes(colour=NA, fill="grey20", size=0.5,
linetype=1, weight = 1, alpha = 1)

   required_aes <- c("x", "y")

   reparameterise <- function(., df, params) {
     df$width <- df$width %||%
       params$width %||% (resolution(df$y, FALSE) * 0.9)
     transform(df,
       xmin = pmin(x, 0), xmax = pmax(x, 0),
       ymin = y - width / 2, ymax = y + width / 2, width = NULL
     )
   }

   draw_groups <- function(., data, scales, coordinates, ...) {
     GeomRect$draw_groups(data, scales, coordinates, ...)
   }

   # Documentation -----------------------------------------------
   objname <- "hbar"
   desc <- "Bars, rectangles with bases on y-axis"
   guide_geom <- function(.) "polygon"

   icon <- function(.) {
     rectGrob(c(0.3, 0.7), c(0.4, 0.8), height=c(0.4, 0.8), width=0.3,
vjust=1, gp=gpar(fill="grey20", col=NA))
   }
})
geom_hbar <- GeomHbar$build_accessor()

p.hbar <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = proportion, y = item)) +
   geom_hbar() +

   facet_grid(type ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free") +

   opts(title = "Good, actual horizontal bars")

p.hbar

Note that geom_hbar is not nearly as general as geom_bar; for one thing
its default stat is identity, not bin.  There isn't a stat which bins
along the y axis (although you could write one), so if you try to change
the stat to bin, I don't really know what would happen.  Basically, I
just took geom_bar, flipped the x and y in the reparameterise function,

>>> Hi people,
>>>
>>> # I'm trying to produce a faceted plot with horizontal bars and I
>>> # can't seem to get what I want. If you copy and paste everything below
>>> you'll
>>> # get one plot containing my three attempts. For more detail see comments
>>> below.
>>>
>>> # Here's my working example:
>>>
>>> require(ggplot2)
>>>
>>> # fake data
>>> dat<- data.frame(
>>>    type = c(rep("Veg", 4), rep("Fruit",2)),
>>>    item = c("Potato", "Spinach", "Red onion", "Mixed leaves", "Tomato",
>>> "Lime"),
>>>    proportion = c(0.03, 0.35, 0.95, 0.2, 0.57, 0.01)
>>> )
>>> dat$item<- reorder(dat$item, dat$proportion)
>>>
>>>
>>> # First off, it's easy enough to produce the dot plot of what I want, so
>>> let's
>>> # do that:
>>>
>>> p.dot<- ggplot(dat, aes(x = proportion, y = item)) +
>>>    geom_point() +
>>>    facet_grid(type ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free") +
>>>    opts(title = "Good, but I want bars not dots")
>>>
>>> p.dot
>>>
>>> # However, what I'm really after is a bar version of 'p.dot', so instead
>> of
>>> dots
>>> # we have horizontal bars starting out from zero. I can try and get this
>> by
>>> # doing something similar and using coord_flip():
>>>
>>> p.bar<- ggplot(dat, aes(x = item, y = proportion)) +   # x and y are
>>> opposite
>>>    geom_bar() +
>>>    coord_flip() +
>>>    facet_grid(type ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free") +

>>>

>>>

>>> # in for each category, we didn't have that problem in 'p.dot'

>> and / or column in the facet, not for individual "cells" in the facet.
>> And then it gets confused by coord_flip, and doesn't realize that the
>> rows and columns have switched.
>>
>> There is already a bug report open on this issue
>> (https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/95) so hopefully it will be
>> fixed soon. In the meantime the closest I can get is
>>
>> ggplot(dat, aes(x = item, y = proportion)) +
>>   geom_bar() +
>>    facet_wrap(~ type, scales = "free", ncol = 1) +
>>   coord_flip()
>>
>>
>> HTH,

Hello

By default, it seems ggplot2 uses scale_colour_hue() (see book, page 106). I would like however to change this default, so that it uses my own scale scale_fill_manual(value = 1:7). How can I do it globally? Locally I can always add:
qplot(color, data = diamonds, fill=color,geom = "bar")+scale_fill_manual(value = 1:7)

but I would like the change to be global... i.e., by default qplot uses my scale, instead of scale_fill_hue(). I had a look at theme_update() and update_geom_defaults() but these do not concern the scale_fill... Is it possible to do it globally, or do I have to do it locally each time?

Thanks!

Matthieu

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

probably this is problem of install.packages in windows.

install_github finally calls install.packages with type="source", so
probably the problem occurs in the install.packages in windows.
install.package with type="source" internally calls R CMD INSTALL as
shell command, and, in windows, the path-to-library is set via system
environment variable, i.e., Sys.setenv.

So, it may be helpful:

1. debug(install.package)
2. call install_github
3. in debug mode, run just before shell command: the line, if (system(cmd) > 0L)
4. inspect the cmd
5. inspect the system environment variable by Sys.getenv()

if these works,

Sys.setenv(HOGE="hoge")
Sys.getenv("HOGE")
system("set") # In my memory, "set" is windows counterpart of bash
"export." anyway, call the command showing environment variables.

and inspect the output. It should contain something like HOGE=hoge.

Probably I can test these in a few days.

--
Kohske Takahashi <takahash...@gmail.com>

Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology,
The University of  Tokyo, Japan.
http://www.fennel.rcast.u-tokyo.ac.jp/profilee_ktakahashi.html

Hello,

I am a new R users.  Mimicing the SAS macro, I have written the
following R function to produce pdf output of several bar plots using
ggplot geom_bar from one run.

an error Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'yvar' not found

I would appreciate receiving your help debug the program.

Thanks,

Pradip

#### The R Script begins here ####
setwd ("F:/Disorders")
library (ggplot2)

myPlot <- function(lFrame,yTrigger )
{
  yvar = rep(c(0),21)

   lFrame$age <- factor(lFrame$age,
                        labels=c("12-17", "18-25", "26 or Older")

   # In the data frame, race/ethnicity is coded as follows:
   # 1=White, 2=Black, 3=AI/AN, 4="Hawiian/OPI",
   # 5=Asian, 6=Multi Races,7=Hispanic

   lFrame$race <- factor(

(5,2,4,7,1,6,3),

"Hispanic","White",

AN")                         )

   limits <- aes(ymax = yvar_u, ymin=yvar_l)
   print("limits")
   dodge <- position_dodge(width=1)

   p <- ggplot(lFrame, aes(y=yvar, x=race, fill=race ))+
        geom_bar(position=dodge) +
        geom_errorbar(limits, position=dodge, width=0.3) +
        #geom_text (aes(label = abodmrj,colour="black", face="bold"))
+
        facet_wrap(~ age, ncol=3)+
        scale_fill_manual(values=c("brown", "grey", "red",
"lightgreen",

                       )+
        xlab("")+
        ylab("Percentages")+

        opts(legend.position="none",
           panel.grid.major=theme_blank(),
           panel.grid.minor=theme_blank(),
           title="Past-Year Marijuana Use Disorder (2002-2010)",
           axis.text.y=theme_text(size=11, face="bold"),

face="bold"),

}

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's another approach using geom_segment():

ggplot(dat, aes(x = proportion, y = item)) +

  geom_segment(aes(xend = 0, yend = item), size = 10) +

  facet_grid(type ~ ., scales = 'free_y', space = 'free')

All this does is replace geom_point() with the equivalent code in
geom_segment(). Hopefully this is a bit more robust wrt the upcoming
changes in ggplot2.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Include a legend with Greeks letters
messages.subject_clean: Include a legend with Greeks letters
messages.body_plain:
Dear all:

Currently I am creating a graphic using ggplot with the code below.
With the function "geom_text()" I have added the individual means of
each density plot, nevertheless I would like to add in front of the
value a Greek letter  indicating the parameter. I attempt so using the
functions "expression" and "paste" within the "geom_text" function,
but I got a message regarding a missing "aes". I assume that at some
point I should include the function "aes()" nonetheless I have no idea
how.

does anyone has a suggestion on how to do it?

best regards,

Sergio René

### Read data
data<- read.csv("th_Hansen_Seo_1.csv")
mode(data)
attach(data)
names(data)
dim(data)

### call the libraries
library("ggplot2")
library(reshape)

### generates the labels in greek letters
my.labs<-list(bquote(beta==hat(beta)),bquote(beta==1))

### creates data subsets
data1=subset(data, abs(Threshold)<25) #### for looking the [-25,25]
window
data_250=subset(data,t<251) ##### subsets for 250
data_500=subset(data,t>251) ##### subsets for 500
data_250_0=subset(data_250, Restriction<1) #### subset 250 no
restriction on Beta
data_250_1=subset(data_250, Restriction>0) #### subset 250 restriction
on Beta
data_500_0=subset(data_500, Restriction<1) #### subset 250 no
restriction on Beta
data_500_1=subset(data_500, Restriction>0) #### subset 250 restriction
on Beta

### creates mean values for each subset
dfs_250_0<-recast(data_250_0,p.value+Pi~variable, fun.aggregate=mean)
dfs_250_1<-recast(data_250_1,p.value+Pi~variable, fun.aggregate=mean)
dfs_500_0<-recast(data_500_0,p.value+Pi~variable, fun.aggregate=mean)
dfs_500_1<-recast(data_500_1,p.value+Pi~variable, fun.aggregate=mean)

### True threshold

value=-2

#### creates the graphic for 250 observations
d <- qplot(Threshold,data=subset(data_250,abs(Threshold)<30),
geom="density", colour=Beta) +
	facet_wrap(p.value~Pi)+
	xlab(expression(theta))+
	scale_colour_manual(values=1:2,breaks=c("b=b","b=1"),labels=my.labs)+
	geom_vline(data=dfs_250_0, aes(xintercept=Threshold), color="red")+
	geom_vline(data=dfs_250_1, aes(xintercept=Threshold), color="black")+
	geom_vline(xintercept=-2, color="blue")+
	geom_text(data=dfs_250_0, aes(x=8,y=0.3, label=round(Threshold,
2)),size=3, colour="red")+
	geom_text(data=dfs_250_1, aes(x=8,y=0.25, label=round(Threshold,
2)),size=3, colour="black")+
	geom_text(aes(x=8, y= 0.35, label=value), size=3, colour="blue")

grob <- ggplotGrob(d)

strip_elem <- grid.ls <http://grid.ls>(getGrob(grob, "strip.text.x", grep=TRUE,
global=TRUE))$name

grob <- geditGrob(grob, strip_elem[1],
label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.10",", ",pi[0],"=0.05")))
grob <- geditGrob(grob, strip_elem[2],
label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.05",", ",pi[0],"=0.05")))
grob <- geditGrob(grob, strip_elem[3],
label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.01",", ",pi[0],"=0.05")))
grob <- geditGrob(grob, strip_elem[4],
label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.10",", ",pi[0],"=0.10")))
grob <- geditGrob(grob, strip_elem[5],
label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.05",", ",pi[0],"=0.10")))
grob <- geditGrob(grob, strip_elem[6],
label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.01",", ",pi[0],"=0.10")))
grob <- geditGrob(grob, strip_elem[7],
label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.10",", ",pi[0],"=0.15")))
grob <- geditGrob(grob, strip_elem[8],
label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.05",", ",pi[0],"=0.15")))
grob <- geditGrob(grob, strip_elem[9],
label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.01",", ",pi[0],"=0.15")))

grid.draw(grob)

Glad to be of help.
What a lot of extra code just to handle the windows environment.
R CMD needs a --r-lib option.

On Aug 11, 2:03 am, Hadley Wickham <had...@rice.edu> wrote:
> Hmmm, I guess I didn't realise R CMD build needed to access the

> required packages.  New issue athttps://github.com/hadley/devtools/issues/24 <http://github.com/hadley/devtools/issues/24>

>
> hadley
>
> On Thu, Aug 11, 2011 at 5:03 AM, Kohske Takahashi
>

>
> > --

> > Kohske Takahashi <takahashi.koh...@gmail.com>

>
> > Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology,
> > The University of  Tokyo, Japan.
> >http://www.fennel.rcast.u-tokyo.ac.jp/profilee_ktakahashi.html
>

> > On Thu, Aug 11, 2011 at 8:02 AM, peta <pwha...@bhvr.com> wrote:
> >> I found that install.packages(type=source) is not called in this case.
> >> Instead it uses devtools::build where it tries to run R CMD build.
> >> I have no R startup files so build has no clue that dependency packages have
> >> been installed in a non-standard place.
> >> The R_LIBS environment variable is not set.
> >> As a quick hack, Sys.setenv(R_LIBS=.filePaths()[1]) before the R(cmd,path)
> >> worked.
>
> >>> build
> >> function (pkg = NULL, path = NULL, binary = FALSE)
> >> {
> >>     pkg <- as.package(pkg)
> >>     if (is.null(path)) {
> >>         path <- dirname(pkg$path)
> >>     }
> >>     if (binary) {
> >>         cmd <- paste("CMD INSTALL ", shQuote(pkg$path), " --build",
> >>             sep = "")
> >>         ext <- if (os() == "win")
> >>             "zip"
> >>         else "tgz"
> >>     }
> >>     else {
> >>         cmd <- paste("CMD build ", shQuote(pkg$path), " --no-manual
> >> --no-vignettes",
> >>             sep = "")
> >>         ext <- "tar.gz"
> >>     }
> >>     R(cmd, path)
> >>     targz <- paste(pkg$package, "_", pkg$version, ".", ext, sep = "")
> >>     file.path(path, targz)
> >> }
> >> <environment: namespace:devtools>
> >> In install.packages the R_LIBS are setup up like this to take into account
> >> the different platforms,
> >> so I guess something similar needs to take place in devtools::build as well.

messages.subject: shifted spectra with colour labels
messages.subject_clean: shifted spectra with colour labels
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I've spent some time tweaking ggplot2 for the attached plot, using
directlabels and geom_text, but finally resorted to a hack shown
below. I'm curious to hear if

- this kind of plot has a name

- I missed a more obvious way to achieve the same end result. In
particular, I am not happy with the step where the colors are
hard-coded in the data, and plotted with scale_colour_identity. This
was necessary to obtain the same colours for the y-axis labels, which
I could not otherwise get to stand outside the plot area when using
geom_text().

The data consist in multiple spectra taken at different times. I wish
to plot them with a common axis, and offset them regularly along the
(arbitrary units) y axis to avoid undesirable overlap between
successive lines. The idea behind the representation is to see a trend
in spectral features such as peak shifts or (dis)appearance of peaks.

All the best,

baptiste

Here's a plot of the data,

library(hyperSpec)
plot(laser)

and now the ggplot2 hack to shift the spectra, plot them in gradual
colors, and label the different times with the corresponding colors,

library(hyperSpec)
library(ggplot2)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(scales)

## unobtrusive theme to focus on the spectra
theme_minimal <- function (base_size = 12, base_family = "", ...){
  modifyList(ggplot2::theme_bw (base_size = base_size, base_family =
base_family),
             list (axis.line = theme_blank(),
                   legend.background = theme_rect(colour = NA),
                   legend.key = theme_rect(colour = NA),
                   panel.background = theme_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
                   panel.border = theme_blank(),
                   strip.background = theme_blank(),
                   plot.background = theme_blank()))
}

## define a color palette function
palet <- gradient_n_pal(brewer.pal(3, "Set1")[c(2,1,3)])

##' shift the origin of spectra to avoid y overlap
## and hard-code the colors associated with each time step
spreadplot <- function(x, colors = palet, s=1){

  test <- apply(x[[]], 2, diff)
  shift <- max(-test[test < 0])
  x$origins <- s*seq(0, by=shift, length=nrow(x))
  x$scale <- colors(scales::rescale(x$origins))
  x

}

## make a long format data.frame
toplot <- as.long.df(spreadplot(laser))

## select every other time step for the labels
lab <- subset(toplot, .wavelength == max(toplot$.wavelength) &
              t %in%  t[seq(1, length(t), by=2)])
levs <- unique(lab$origins)
lab.colors <- palet(rescale(levs))

p <-
ggplot(toplot) +
  geom_path(aes(.wavelength, spc + origins, colour=scale, group=t)) +
  scale_colour_identity()+
  labs(x= expression("wavelength / nm"), y="I / a.u.", colour="t / s") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks=levs, labels=round(lab$t, 1), expand=c(0,0)) +
  opts(axis.text.y = theme_text(size = 8, hjust=1, colour=lab.colors))+
  opts(legend.position="none")

p

messages.subject: Circular density plots
messages.subject_clean: Circular density plots
messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody.

I'm struggling with density estimation for my (circular ~ time) data.
Here is some simulated data, but it return the same error message as
my real data-set:

require(circular)
require(ggplot2)

set.seed(123)
X = rbeta(100, shape1 = 2, shape2 = 4)
X = 2 * pi * X
X = circular(X, type = "angle", units = "radians", rotation = "clock")
X = as.data.frame.circular(X)
p <- ggplot(X, aes(x = x))
p <- p + geom_histogram(aes(y = ..count..))
p <- p + coord_polar(theta = "x", start = 2*pi, direction = 1, expand
= FALSE)
print(p)

#Error in if (test == TRUE) { : argument is of length zero

Yet it works when using native circular methods:

set.seed(123)
X = rbeta(100, shape1 = 2, shape2 = 4)
X = 2 * pi * X
X = circular(X, type = "angle", units = "radians", rotation = "clock")
rose.diag(X, bins = 12, shrink = 0.33, xlim = c(-2, 2), ylim = c(-2,
2), axes = FALSE,
          prop = 1.5)

#or kernel density estimation:
set.seed(123)
X = rbeta(100, shape1 = 2, shape2 = 4)
X = 2 * pi * X
X = circular(X, type = "angle", units = "radians", rotation = "clock")
plot.circular(X, stack = TRUE, shrink = 0.35, cex = 0, sep = 0.0, axes
= FALSE,
     tol = .8, zero = c(0), bins = 12, xlim = c(-2, 2), ylim = c (-2,
2),
     ticks = TRUE, tcl = .075)
vonmises = density.circular(X, kernel = "vonmises", n = 512, bw = 300)
lines(vonmises, col = "darkgrey", lwd = 3)

# use vonmises and convert it into data.frame before calling ggplot2

p + geom_line() + coord_polar(theta = "x", start = 2*pi, direction =

messages.body_plain:
I have a function that creates a ggplot graphic based on several
parameters and the saves the graphic to a png or pdf by calling the
pdf/png(), print(), and dev.off() functions. This is working great.

However, when I save the graphic, it prints it with a screen size
equal to the default unmaximized screen that shows up by just calling
a generic plot. My graphics are less overplotted/cluttered when I
maximize the plot viewing window inside of the standard R GUI.

How can I modify the pdf/png or print functions so that they will
print the maximized version of the graphic instead of the default
unmaximized version?

I know I can adjust the height, width, and resolution manually inside
of the pdf.png functions. However, I am having trouble finding the
optimal parameters. I feel it would be easier to just have some sort
of maximized screen setting size.

Thank you everyone in advance for your help! The relevant portion of
the code is included below:

    emp_proficiency_plot <- ggplot(emp_subset, aes(x = date, y =
total_freq,
      label = area, colour = date, size = total_freq)) +
      geom_text(position = position_jitter(height=3, width = 0)) +
      scale_size(to = c(2, 5)) +
      opts(axis.text.x = theme_blank()) +
      opts(axis.text.y = theme_blank()) +
      xlab(paste("Employee:", parameter)) + ylab("Competency
Proficiency") +
      opts(title = paste("Employee Competencies by Date:",
        pub_date_start, "-", pub_date_end)) +
      labs(colour = "Date") + labs(size = "Frequency")

    pdf("C:/Users/bjvanov/Desktop/tester.pdf")
    print(emp_proficiency_plot)
    dev.off()}

messages.body_plain:
Dear all, sorry for the double posting. I was recommended to include
on the code provided an example of the data used. As for that I
included a set of artificial data for my example.
I am working with simulations and I am plotting the densities of
estimated parameters (thresholds) using two time dimensions lengths,
250 and 500. The shape of the distribution is separated on the basis
of the level of significance of the estimated parameter (p.value) and
a trimming parameter (Pi). Furthermore the estimation can be done with
and without restriction.
What I want to do is add to each density not only the line and values
of the "true", "average with restriction" and "average without
restriction" threshold parameters. But also I would like to add near
to each value a Greek letter showing the parameter, i.e.
"theta[beta=1]". I am wondering if there is a way to do this using the
function "geom_text". I tried by combining such a function with the
functions "expression" and "paste" but does not work. does anyone has
an idea on how to achieve such result?

All the best,

Sergio René Araujo-Enciso

##### Example non-actual data
Threshold<-rnorm(7200,-2,1)
p.value<-rep(c(rep(c("p.value=0.9"),12),rep(c("p.value=0.95"),
12),rep(c("p.value=0.99"),12)),200)#### level of significance
Pi<-rep(c(rep(c("p=0.05"),4),rep(c("p=0.01"),4),rep(c("p=0.15"),4)),
600) ##### trimming parameter
Beta<-rep(c(rep(c("b=1"),2),rep(c("b=b"),2)),1800) #### label for
restriction
Restriction<-rep(c(rep(c(1),2),rep(c(0),2)),1800)#### value for
restriction
t<-rep(c(250,500),3600)
data<-data.frame(Threshold, p.value, Pi, Beta, Restriction, t)

### call the libraries
library("ggplot2")
library(reshape)

### generates the labels in greek letters
my.labs<-list(bquote(beta==hat(beta)),bquote(beta==1))

#### generated sub-datasets

data_250=subset(data,t<251) ##### subsets for 250
data_500=subset(data,t>251) ##### subsets for 500
data_250_0=subset(data_250, Restriction<1) #### subset 250 no
restriction on Beta
data_250_1=subset(data_250, Restriction>0) #### subset 250 restriction
on Beta
data_500_0=subset(data_500, Restriction<1) #### subset 250 no
restriction on Beta
data_500_1=subset(data_500, Restriction>0) #### subset 250 restriction
on Beta

### creates mean values for each subset
dfs_250_0<-recast(data_250_0,p.value+Pi~variable, fun.aggregate=mean)
dfs_250_1<-recast(data_250_1,p.value+Pi~variable, fun.aggregate=mean)
dfs_500_0<-recast(data_500_0,p.value+Pi~variable, fun.aggregate=mean)
dfs_500_1<-recast(data_500_1,p.value+Pi~variable, fun.aggregate=mean)

### True threshold
value=-2

#### creates the graphic for 250 observations

plot_250 <- qplot(Threshold,data=subset(data_250,abs(Threshold)<30),

geom="density", colour=Beta) +
	facet_wrap(p.value~Pi)+
	xlab(expression(theta))+
	scale_colour_manual(values=1:2,breaks=c("b=b","b=1"),labels=my.labs)+
	geom_vline(data=dfs_250_0, aes(xintercept=Threshold), color="red")+
	geom_vline(data=dfs_250_1, aes(xintercept=Threshold), color="black")+
	geom_vline(xintercept=-2, color="blue")+

	geom_text(data=dfs_250_0, aes(x=4,y=0.3, label=round(Threshold,
2)),size=4,colour="red")+
	geom_text(data=dfs_250_1, aes(x=4,y=0.25, label=round(Threshold,
2)),size=4,colour="black")+
	geom_text(aes(x=4, y= 0.35, label=value), size=4, colour="blue")

grob_250 <- ggplotGrob(plot_250)

strip_elem_250 <- grid.ls <http://grid.ls>(getGrob(grob_250, "strip.text.x", grep=TRUE,
global=TRUE))$name

grob_250 <- geditGrob(grob_250, strip_elem_250[1],

label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.10",", ",pi[0],"=0.05")))

grob_250 <- geditGrob(grob_250, strip_elem_250[2],

label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.05",", ",pi[0],"=0.05")))

grob_250 <- geditGrob(grob_250, strip_elem_250[3],

label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.01",", ",pi[0],"=0.05")))

grob_250 <- geditGrob(grob_250, strip_elem_250[4],

label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.10",", ",pi[0],"=0.10")))

grob_250 <- geditGrob(grob_250, strip_elem_250[5],

label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.05",", ",pi[0],"=0.10")))

grob_250 <- geditGrob(grob_250, strip_elem_250[6],

label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.01",", ",pi[0],"=0.10")))

grob_250 <- geditGrob(grob_250, strip_elem_250[7],

label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.10",", ",pi[0],"=0.15")))

grob_250 <- geditGrob(grob_250, strip_elem_250[8],

label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.05",", ",pi[0],"=0.15")))

grob_250 <- geditGrob(grob_250, strip_elem_250[9],

label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.01",", ",pi[0],"=0.15")))

#### Save the graphic for 250 observations
png(file="Hansen_Seo_Test_Threshold_250.png", bg="transparent", width
= 460, height = 460)
grid.draw(grob_250)
dev.off()

### creates graphic for 500 observations

plot_500 <- qplot(Threshold,data=subset(data_500,abs(Threshold)<15),

geom="density", colour=Beta) +
	facet_wrap(p.value~Pi)+
	xlab(expression(theta))+
	scale_colour_manual(values=1:2,breaks=c("b=b","b=1"),labels=my.labs)+

	geom_vline(data=dfs_500_0, aes(xintercept=Threshold), color="red")+
	geom_vline(data=dfs_500_1, aes(xintercept=Threshold), color="black")+
	geom_vline(xintercept=-2, color="blue")+
	geom_text(data=dfs_500_0, aes(x=4,y=0.3, label=round(Threshold,
2)),size=4,colour="red")+
	geom_text(data=dfs_500_1, aes(x=4,y=0.25, label=round(Threshold,
2)),size=4,colour="black")+
	geom_text(aes(x=4, y= 0.35, label=value), size=4,colour="blue")

grob_500 <- ggplotGrob(plot_500)

label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.10",", ",pi[0],"=0.15")))

label=expression(paste(alpha,"=0.05",", ",pi[0],"=0.15")))

> I am working with simulations and I am plotting the densities of
> estimated parameters (thresholds) using two time dimensions lengths,
> 250 and 500. The shape of the distribution is separated on the basis
> of the level of significance of the estimated parameter (p.value) and
> a trimming parameter (Pi). Furthermore the estimation can be done with
> and without restriction.
> What I want to do is add to each density not only the line and values
> of the "true", "average with restriction" and "average without
> restriction" threshold parameters. But also I would like to add near
> to each value a Greek letter showing the parameter, i.e.
> "theta[beta=1]". I am wondering if there is a way to do this using the
> function "geom_text". I tried by combining such a function with the
> functions "expression" and "paste" but does not work. does anyone has
> an idea on how to achieve such result?

You want to add parse=TRUE to the geom_text call.  Then it will treat
the label as an expression:

ggplot(data.frame(x=c(0,1),y=c(1,0)), aes(x,y)) +
	geom_point() +
	geom_text(aes(x=0.5, y=0.5,
			label=paste("theta[beta==1] == ", -2, sep="")),
		parse=TRUE)

See more comments below.

> All the best,
>
> Sergio Ren� Araujo-Enciso
>

Your example was complete, but lengthy and involved a lot more than what
was needed to answer your question.  In fact, I answered something
completely different before realizing that wasn't what you asked.  I
thought you were asking about making the labels in the facets correct

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hello Derrick,

It's a seconds vs. days issue I bet.

My understanding is that as.Date will make it in days from 1/1/1970 and POSIXct will be in seconds.  This will make is so your scales won't match.  Scale your values with 86400 and it might work.

To explore this you can type in as.numeric(as.Date("2011-06-01"))
To explore this you can type in as.numeric(as.POSIXct("2011-06-01"r))

Cheers,
Jonathan

messages.subject: Re: geom_density legend symbols
messages.subject_clean: geom_density legend symbols
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I'm not sure this is what you had in mind, but consider the following example:

dd <- data.frame(gp = factor(rep(1:5, each = 100)), y = rnorm(500))
ggplot(dd, aes(x = y, fill = gp, colour = gp)) +
   theme_bw() +
   geom_density(alpha = 0.3)  +
   scale_colour_manual(breaks = levels(dd$gp), values = NA)

The last line of code removes the outlines from the legend but also
from the plot. The alpha transparency is to avoid (partial) obscurity
of one density plot by another.

HTH,
Dennis

hi,

using dev version and Dennis's sample, you can remove the line and set
alpha of legend to 1.0 like this:

dd <- data.frame(gp = factor(rep(1:5, each = 100)), y = rnorm(500))
ggplot(dd, aes(x = y, fill = gp, colour = gp)) +
 theme_bw() +
 geom_density(alpha = 0.3) +

 guides(fill=guide_legend(set.aes=list(colour=NULL, alpha=1)))

find how to install here: https://gist.github.com/1139848

of extension that I thought would be most used (creating new theme_XXX

have some sort of inheritance so that axis.text.x would inherit
properties from axis, text and x theme components.

messages.subject_clean: ggsave: y-axis label is moved around depending on width and height options of ggsave
messages.body_plain:
Dear ggplot2-expeRts,

The following plot looks fine, but when I specify widht and height and
save it
to a file it shifts the y axis label. Is this a bug or a feature?

library(ggplot2)
df <- data.frame(Year=rep(2001:2010,3), Number=sample(x=1:100,
size=3*10, replace=TRUE),
                 Group=rep(1:3, each=10))
p <- ggplot(df, aes(x=Year, y=Number, fill=Group)) +
geom_bar(stat="identity",
                                      position="stack", binwidth=1) +
    opts(aspect.ratio=1/2, title="My title",
         legend.position="bottom", legend.direction="horizontal") +
    labs(x="My xlab", y="My ylab")
p # looks fine
ggsave("barplot.pdf") # also fine
ggsave("barplot.pdf", width=15, height=5) # why does it move the y
axis label so much to the left?

Cheers,

Marius

Your example looks fairly simple.

x data would be your variables. (e.g. points per game)
y data would be the value of those variables (without scaling this might not work very well)
The color could be specified by another variable.

Facet by team and you're there.

dataframe would be in this structure

bball<-structure(list(Team = structure(c(1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L), .Label = c("Dallas",
"Miami"), class = "factor"), Variable = structure(c(2L, 3L, 1L,
2L, 3L, 1L), .Label = c("Dunks", "PPG", "Rebounds"), class = "factor"),
    Value = c(90L, 15L, 20L, 90L, 25L, 10L), Col = c(1L, 2L,
    1L, 2L, 1L, 2L)), .Names = c("Team", "Variable", "Value",
"Col"), class = "data.frame", row.names = c(NA, -6L))

ggplot(bball, aes(x=Variable, y=Value, fill=as.factor(Col)))+geom_bar()+facet_grid(Team~.)

Unless I'm missing something?

Brandon

messages.subject_clean: How to change only one attribute of theme_text()?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I changed the positioning of the title in the plot below. But all
other "font elements"
are lost (such as the size, for example). Is it possible to *only*
change the position
(or *one* other element) without changeing the other elements of
theme_text?

Of course, one could use theme_get() or look at theme_text() and
extract all the
other properties such as size etc., but that seems tedious to type
(especially
since the positioning often changes for different plots).

Cheers,

Marius

library(ggplot2)
set.seed(1)
df <- data.frame(Year=rep(2001:2009,3), Number=c(1:23,rep(23,4)),
                 Group=rep(1:3, each=9))
ggplot(df, aes(x=Year, y=Number, fill=Group)) +
geom_bar(stat="identity",
                                      position="stack", binwidth=1) +
    opts(aspect.ratio=1/2, title="My title",
	 plot.title=theme_text(hjust=0)) + labs(x="My xlab", y="My ylab")

On 8/14/2011 10:39 PM, BenJWoodcroft wrote:
> Hi,
>
> Firstly thanks to those involved with creation and maintenance of
> ggplot2 - it has really revolutionised how I analyse much of my data,
> and the ease at which I can ask new questions means I can ask more
> than previously.
>
> I have a probably naive question regarding stat_smooth. Basically, I'm
> wondering what exactly the line and standard error represent. The help
> at http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/stat_smooth.html suggests that the method
> is this:
> method: smoothing method (function) to use, eg. lm, glm, gam, loess,
> rlm
>
> However the default is "auto". I don't quite understand what "auto"
> means, though - can someone enlighten me? I was unable to find an
> answer on the help pages or a quick google, but I'm known to be blind
> sometimes.

I'm not sure where (or if) it is documented, but auto is equivalent to
"loess" when there are fewer than 1000 rows in the data and is
equivalent to method="gam", formula=y~s(x, bs="cs") if there are 1000 or
more rows (this function is from the "mgcv" package).

> Thanks in advance,
> ben

--

Oregon Health & Science University

It is on github, under the develop branch.  Something of an outline is
at https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/improving-docs, but that is

install.packages(c("devtools","RCurl"))

version in a separate library so that it doesn't overwrite the released
version.

install "roxygen2" (from CRAN) and "scales" (from github) yourself.

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Works for me. Here's a reproducible example:

dd <- data.frame(x = 1:10, x1 = rnorm(10), x2 = rnorm(10),
                 x3 = rnorm(10), x4 = rnorm(10), y = rnorm(10))
ddm <- melt(dd, id = 'x')

# Not in order of linetypes, but works
ggplot(ddm, aes(x = x, y = value, linetype = variable)) + geom_line()

ggplot(ddm, aes(x = x, y = value, linetype = variable)) + geom_line()
# works
last_plot() + scale_linetype_manual(breaks = levels(ddm$variable),
   values = c('solid', 'dashed', 'dotted', 'dotdash', 'longdash'))
# same as above
last_plot() + scale_linetype_manual(breaks = levels(ddm$variable),
   values = 1:5)

You've got an ancient version of R and ggplot2 is under very active
development, so I would strongly urge you to upgrade to the latest
versions of R and ggplot2.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Below is a bar plot. As Hadley noted (on http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/0946ae817c95e2e8/76b76a833ad31150#76b76a833ad31150)
the alignment issue with the y-label is fixed. I used the development version of
ggplot2 to obtain the desired result. However, I noticed some strange things which
are quite different from the older to the development version of ggplot2. I attached two
screenshots (one taken on Mac OS X 10.6.8 with the develment version of ggplot2 on R
2.13 and the other with the current CRAN version of ggplot2 on R 2.14_devel).

(1) I was quite happy to see that the x-axis, y-axis, and title are perfectly
    aligned with respect to the gray background (development version of ggplot2)
    as Hadley wrote (well done!). However, the legend when legend.position="bottom" (or legend.position=c(0.5,0))
    is not perfectly centered with respect to the gray background or with respect

messages.body_plain:
I have typically been using this for cumulative density functions of
game server session lifetimes (http://www.monkeyquest.com).
The session lifetimes can range from seconds to hours, hence the log time scale.

    ggplot(d)
     + geom_line(size=1,aes(x=lifetime,y=percent,color=qos))
     + scale_x_logtime(name=xlab)

Looking at the new code I guess I do this...

    scale_x_logtime <- function(...) {
        scale_x_continuous(..., trans = log10_trans(), breaks = logtime.breaks, labels = logtime.labels)
    }

where logtime.breaks and labels are functions that take limits as an arg.

But what is the right way to handle the minor breaks?
Its important that the time units be "friendly" seconds, minutes and hours
so for example they go 10,20,30,40,50 secs, then jump to 1min, 2min, 3min, etc.
I see there is an internal function scale_breaks_minor but I doubt it will produce what I want.
How do I override that just for my scale?
Do I need to create a new S3 coord and handle that in coord_train?

> Dear list,
>
> I've spent some time tweaking ggplot2 for the attached plot, using
> directlabels and geom_text, but finally resorted to a hack shown
> below. I'm curious to hear if
>
> - this kind of plot has a name
>
> - I missed a more obvious way to achieve the same end result. In
> particular, I am not happy with the step where the colors are
> hard-coded in the data, and plotted with scale_colour_identity. This
> was necessary to obtain the same colours for the y-axis labels, which
> I could not otherwise get to stand outside the plot area when using
> geom_text().
>
> The data consist in multiple spectra taken at different times. I wish
> to plot them with a common axis, and offset them regularly along the
> (arbitrary units) y axis to avoid undesirable overlap between
> successive lines. The idea behind the representation is to see a trend
> in spectral features such as peak shifts or (dis)appearance of peaks.
>
> All the best,
>
> baptiste
>
> Here's a plot of the data,
>
> library(hyperSpec)
> plot(laser)
>
> and now the ggplot2 hack to shift the spectra, plot them in gradual
> colors, and label the different times with the corresponding colors,
>
> library(hyperSpec)
> library(ggplot2)
> library(RColorBrewer)
> library(scales)
>
> ## unobtrusive theme to focus on the spectra
> theme_minimal <- function (base_size = 12, base_family = "", ...){
>  modifyList(ggplot2::theme_bw (base_size = base_size, base_family =
> base_family),
>             list (axis.line = theme_blank(),
>                   legend.background = theme_rect(colour = NA),
>                   legend.key = theme_rect(colour = NA),
>                   panel.background = theme_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
>                   panel.border = theme_blank(),
>                   strip.background = theme_blank(),
>                   plot.background = theme_blank()))
> }
>
> ## define a color palette function
> palet <- gradient_n_pal(brewer.pal(3, "Set1")[c(2,1,3)])
>
> ##' shift the origin of spectra to avoid y overlap
> ## and hard-code the colors associated with each time step
> spreadplot <- function(x, colors = palet, s=1){
>
>  test <- apply(x[[]], 2, diff)
>  shift <- max(-test[test < 0])
>  x$origins <- s*seq(0, by=shift, length=nrow(x))
>  x$scale <- colors(scales::rescale(x$origins))
>  x
>
> }
>
> ## make a long format data.frame
> toplot <- as.long.df(spreadplot(laser))
>
> ## select every other time step for the labels
> lab <- subset(toplot, .wavelength == max(toplot$.wavelength) &
>              t %in%  t[seq(1, length(t), by=2)])
> levs <- unique(lab$origins)
> lab.colors <- palet(rescale(levs))
>
> p <-
> ggplot(toplot) +
>  geom_path(aes(.wavelength, spc + origins, colour=scale, group=t)) +
>  scale_colour_identity()+
>  labs(x= expression("wavelength / nm"), y="I / a.u.", colour="t / s") +
>  theme_minimal() +
>  scale_y_continuous(breaks=levs, labels=round(lab$t, 1), expand=c(0,0)) +
>  opts(axis.text.y = theme_text(size = 8, hjust=1, colour=lab.colors))+
>  opts(legend.position="none")
>
> p

Hi everyone,

I have a question about x-axis tick marks and the positioning of axis
text when using a facet grid.

I'm using the following as part of a function (p1 is a plot that was
previously defined):

p1 <- p1 + facet_grid(X1 ~ hierarchy, space="free", scales="free_x")
p1 <- p1 + opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(angle=45, size=8, hjust=1),
legend.position="none")

When I do this, the tick marks for the x-axis are offset from the
bottom of the x-axis by a different amount for each facet, depending
on the length of the labels associated with each tick mark. If I set
angle=0, this does not happen, but my x-axis labels then become
unreadable.

What is particularly bizarre about this behavior is that it only
happens when I generate this plot using R installed on Linux. Using
the exact same function on a Mac gives x-axis tick marks/labels that
are aligned perfectly. I am using v0.8.9.

Any thoughts?

Thanks in advance!
Miriam

messages.body_plain:
Dear Kohske,

thank you very much for answering. I think you refer to the "update_element" function? I tried the code below. It did not change the title position. I also tried colour=20 as in the examples, but that did not work either.
If this works, then I guess this is a rather useful function. Do you plan to put it in the package (if only the source code / non-exported)?

Cheers,

Marius

require(plyr)
library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(Year=rep(2001:2009,3), Number=c(1:23,rep(23,4)),
                Group=rep(1:3, each=9))

## with update_element from https://github.com/kohske/ggplot2/blob/002e510d0ad80fd3ee4701678b06a30b0aae949f/R/theme.r

##' Update contents of a theme
##'
##' @title Update theme param
##' @param name name of a theme element
##' @param ... Pairs of name and value of theme parameters.
##' @return Updated theme element
##' @export
##' @example
##' x <- theme_text(size = 15)
##' update_element(x, colour = "red")
##' # Partial matching works
##' update_element(x, col = "red")
##' # So does positional
##' update_element(x, "Times New Roman")
##' # And it throws an error if you use an argument that doesn't exist
##' update_element(x, noargument = 12)
##' # Or multiple arguments with the same name
##' update_element(x, size = 12, size = 15)
##'
##' # Will look up element if given name
##' update_element("axis.text.x", colour = 20)
##' # Throws error if incorrectly named
##' update_element("axis.text", colour = 20)
update_element <- function(name, ...) {
 if (is.character(name)) {
   ele <- theme_get()[[name]]
   if (is.null(ele)) {
     stop("Could not find theme element ", name, call. = FALSE)
   }
 } else {
   ele <- name
 }

 call <- attr(ele, "call")
 stopifnot(!is.null(call))

 # Partial matching of named ... args with full names
 f <- eval(call[[1]])
 new_args <- match.call()
 new_args$name <- NULL
 new_args <- as.list(match.call(f, new_args)[-1])

 # Combine old call with new args
 old <- as.list(call)

 # evaluate old args in its env
 evaled_old_args <- llply(names(old[-1]), get, environment(ele))
 names(evaled_old_args) <- names(old[-1])
 # replace premise with evaluated vars
 old <- modifyList(old, evaled_old_args)

 eval(as.call(modifyList(old, new_args)))
}

## now:

ggplot(df, aes(x=Year, y=Number, fill=Group)) +
geom_bar(stat="identity", position="stack", binwidth=1) +

   opts(aspect.ratio=1/2, title="My title", update_element("plot.title", hjust=0)) +

labs(x="My xlab", y="My ylab")

On Aug 15, 1:50 pm, Hadley Wickham <had...@rice.edu> wrote:
> You should be able to do what you want by manually specifying the
> limits on all scales.  A reproducible example is likely to yield
> better answers.

Thank you very much for your answer. I already gave my presentation
and these minor aesthaetic problems of course did not hurt.

My problem was that the plot canvas has different sizes/positions
depending on the size of the legend - which is determined by the
factor name.
align.plots successfully aligns the panels on the same plot.
I would have liked to split this aligned plot now - with the same size
of the panel - into separate files. Then the plots would not jump
around during
the presentation where I say something like: "at1" does not correlate
with the increase /next slide/ but "longAttribute" does correlate.

Example:
library("ggplot2")
library("ggExtra")
df <- data.frame(ids=LETTERS[1:10],value=1:10,at1=rep(c("A","B"),
5),longAttributeName=rep(c("C","D")))
pat1 <- ggplot(df, aes(ids,value)) + geom_point() +
scale_y_continuous("measured",limits=c(0,10)) +
aes(colour=factor(at1))
plat <- ggplot(df, aes(ids,value)) + geom_point() +
scale_y_continuous("measured",limits=c(0,10)) +
aes(colour=factor(longAttributeName))
pat1
plat
align.plots(pat1 + opts(axis.text.x = theme_blank())+xlab(""), plat)

thank you very much,
ido

messages.subject: Re: Problem of alpha() with plot.background panel
messages.subject_clean: Problem of alpha() with plot.background panel
messages.body_plain:
Mat,

when you use alpha blending for colors, the alpha value adds up, if you plot objects on top of each other.
That's the reason why you get the result you want with a fully saturated colour, but not when you use alpha < 1.

Try to use a transparent background for your plot panel , and you will be fine, i.e.:

library(ggplot2)

alphaCol<-rgb(0.3,0.23,0.34, alpha=0.5) #prob

theme_update(
plot.background = theme_rect(fill = alphaCol),

panel.background = theme_rect(fill = -rgb(0.3,0.23,0.34, alpha=0))
)

qplot(displ, hwy, data = mpg)

Heike
